transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-14
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE); Marcus Chen (Redwood SE); Priya Shah (Atlas BI - Head of Platform); Daniel Morales (Atlas BI - SRE); Evan Lee (Atlas BI - Security); Sara Ito (Atlas BI - PM)

Summary:
Quick demo focused on org/project key model for multi-tenant rate limiting, fairburst allocation, and quota policies via the Console and API. Walked through how to map Atlas BI orgs/projects to Redwood projects, sticky routing for dedicated pools, and pilot scope for benchmarking. Action items captured.

Topics covered:
- Org vs project API key hierarchy
- Fairburst (burst lanes) behavior and backpressure
- Per-project quotas and sticky routing to dedicated capacity
- Console demo: quota slices, quota alerts, and TTLs
- Security: KMS, audit logs, SSO/SAML integration
- Pilot plan and success criteria

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Marcus and I from Redwood. Who do we have on the Atlas side?
[00:08] Priya Shah: Hi, Priya here. Daniel, Evan and Sara are on with me. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:12] Marcus Chen: Awesome. We wanted to show the org/project key patterns we typically recommend for multi-tenant customers, particularly for fairburst and quota isolation. We'll jump into the Console and then the API examples.
[00:24] Daniel Morales: Sounds good. Our main goals today: make sure we can limit noisy tenants, keep latency under 150ms p50 for interactive queries, and quantify cost for reserved vs hosted.
[00:34] Evan Lee: And from security side, we need KMS integration and audit logging — plus, how RBAC maps to keys.
[00:40] Lena Park: Totally. We'll touch those. Quick note: transcription may mangle a few product names — so apologies if you see stuff like 'key-v cache' or 'Redwood Dedicado' in auto notes.
[00:50] Sara Ito: Haha, yeah the transcript is always its own thing.
[00:52] Marcus Chen: Ok, starting with the high-level pattern. We recommend mapping Atlas as an org in Redwood and then creating project keys per internal tenant or product slice. That gives you two levers: org-level quotas for global spend and project-level quotas for per-tenant isolation.
[01:12] Priya Shah: When you say project keys, do they support nested teams? Like we have a few internal workflows that need separate throttles.
[01:20] Marcus Chen: Yes, project keys are flexible — you can create many project tokens under an org. Each token gets its own quota, concurrency limit, and can be routed to different capacity pools. For internal workflows you can either create project keys per workflow or group them and use routing tags.
[01:34] Daniel Morales: How does fairburst work? If we have sustained throughput but occasional spikes, can the system let some tenants exceed quota briefly without affecting others?
[01:44] Lena Park: That's the idea. Fairburst allocates a short-lived burst window based on unused capacity and configured burst lanes. It tries to be fair across active tenants. Important caveat: burst is bounded — if the system is under heavy sustained load, backpressure or fallback kicks in.
[02:00] Marcus Chen: I'll share the Console — bear with me while I switch screens.
[02:06] [screen share sound/noise]
[02:12] Marcus Chen: Here is the org view for 'Atlas-BI' — sorry dummy data. On the left you can see Projects -> Quotas -> Routing. If I click into project 'search-api-prod', you can see quotas: monthly tokens, concurrency cap (2 per key), and a burst window setting.
[02:32] Sara Ito: Can the concurrency cap be per-route or only per-key?
[02:36] Marcus Chen: Today it's per-key, but we support per-route SLO tags that affect routing. We're working on finer-grained per-route throttles in the next quarter.
[02:46] Evan Lee: About routing: we want sticky routing to our dedicated pool for high-priority tenants. If we do dedicated and hosted fallbacks, how do you ensure privacy/tenancy separation?
[02:58] Lena Park: Good question. In Dedicated, you get isolated GPU pools and storage. Routing policies can pin a project key or set of keys to the dedicated pool; if capacity isn't available, you can choose automatic fallback to a compatible model in hosted with audit logs showing that fallback event.
[03:14] Daniel Morales: Are fallbacks logged with request/response IDs? We need that for debugging.
[03:19] Marcus Chen: Yes, every routed request has trace IDs in the Console traces panel; fallback events and reason codes are recorded in the request metadata and our audit logs for compliance.
[03:28] Priya Shah: Ok, show us fairburst behavior in a simulated load — like one tenant spikes.
[03:34] Marcus Chen: Sure. I'll open the load simulation tool — this is in the Optimize tab. You can define tenant distributions, set a burst policy, and see simulated tail latency and token consumption.
[03:44] [ambient keyboard sounds]
[03:50] Marcus Chen: Here I set tenant A to 500 qps sustained, tenant B low, then inject a 60-second spike. You can see the burst pool draw and the fairshare algorithm throttle back tenants as the global pool saturates.
[04:06] Lena Park: It's worth noting the difference between two modes: strict quotas (hard caps) which will return 429s when exceeded, and soft quotas with burst which let you go over temporarily but with throttling precedence rules. Many teams start with soft quotas for UX, then tighten to hard caps once patterns are predictable.
[04:26] Daniel Morales: For our product, user-facing latency matters more than cost for a specific subset of tenants. Is there a way to set priority lanes?
[04:34] Marcus Chen: Yes, priority lanes are supported. You can tag keys as high-priority; routing will attempt to keep them on low-latency pools and give them preferential burst allocation. This is essentially the 'priority policy' you saw in our docs.
[04:46] Priya Shah: How do we map our billing? We want per-team chargebacks. If one tenant uses the burst a lot, do we get visibility?
[04:54] Lena Park: Console has token-level cost breakdowns by project key and route. You can export CSVs or feed to your BI. We also provide per-token unit pricing that can be attached to keys to compute internal chargebacks.
[05:06] Evan Lee: Security question: can project keys be rotated automatically and have per-key RBAC?
[05:12] Marcus Chen: Keys can be rotated via the API or the Console; we support scheduled rotations. For RBAC, you get role mappings at the org level: admin, billing, operator, viewer. You can scope roles to specific projects via the Console UI — the mapping is in the access control panel.
[05:26] Sa... sorry, go ahead Sara.
[05:28] Sara Ito: No, just a quick one: how do we test in our staging? We prefer a staging sandbox where we can use a copy of the data but isolate costs.
[05:36] Lena Park: For staging we recommend using a separate org in Redwood with a limited quota and a dedicated project key. If you need more realistic GPU behavior, we can spin a time-limited dedicated pool for the pilot runs.
[05:48] Daniel Morales: Cost question again — reserved vs hosted. If we commit to a reserved capacity, how does burst work? Can reserved have shared burst with hosted?
[05:58] Marcus Chen: Reserved capacity gives you baseline throughput and lower unit cost. Burst is configurable: you can allow reserved pools to borrow from a shared burst capacity; alternatively, you can allow burst to spill to hosted on overflow. The policy is configurable per org.
[06:12] Priya Shah: Is there an SLA delta when falling back from dedicated to hosted? We have uptime contractual obligations.
[06:18] Lena Park: The SLA for dedicated is higher; fallback to hosted is designed as a safety net but SLA alignment depends on the contract. We'll note SLA expectations in the reserved capacity agreement and include fallback times and notification windows.
[06:30] Evan Lee: About compliance: SOC2 and ISO certs — will you provide the full artifacts and pen test reports?
[06:36] Lena Park: We'll share the SOC2/ISO pack and our latest penetration test summary. For deep audits, we can coordinate an NDA and provide more detailed documentation and egress logs.
[06:48] Marcus Chen: Jumping back to API — quick demo. If you call the inference endpoint with an org header and project API key, the request is charged against project quotas and routed per its policy. Here is a sample curl..
[07:00] Marcus Chen: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer proj_xyz' -H 'X-Redwood-Org: atlas-bi' -d '{"prompt":"query"}' 
[07:12] [minor audio cut]
[07:15] Marcus Chen: Notice the response includes x-redwood-request-id and x-redwood-routing. You can parse those headers for tracing and billing.
[07:24] Daniel Morales: Can we attach per-request metadata so our logs correlate?
[07:28] Marcus Chen: Yes, you can send custom metadata and key-value tags that show up in traces and billing exports. We advise avoiding PII in metadata.
[07:36] Priya Shah: Two quick edge cases: 1) if a project key is compromised, can we invalidate it and failover to a backup? 2) can we split a single tenant across two keys for progressive rollout?
[07:50] Marcus Chen: For (1) you can revoke keys instantly and ensure traffic is rejected; you can also set a fallback key mid-flight but revocation is immediate. For (2) yes, you can use two keys and route a percentage of traffic between them for canary behavior.
[08:04] Evan Lee: How about logs retention for audit — customizable retention windows?
[08:09] Lena Park: Yes, you can set retention per-org up to our max retention (we'll send the exact numbers). For Private/on-prem deployments you manage retention locally.
[08:19] Marcus Chen: I'm going to demo quota slices — this is useful when you want to carve quotas for multiple teams within a project key. You can attach multiple slices with fixed token allocations and priority levels.
[08:32] Sara Ito: Hmm we might use slices for internal dev vs prod workloads.
[08:36] Marcus Chen: Exactly. Slices give you flexibility without creating too many keys.
[08:40] [brief pause, slight cross-talk]
[08:45] Priya Shah: Let's talk about pilot success criteria. For us: 1) maintain p50 <150ms, p95 <500ms for high-priority tenants; 2) no unauthorized data exfiltration; 3) cost model clarity.
[08:58] Lena Park: Good criteria. For the pilot we propose a 2-week run in staging: we'll mirror a subset of traffic (you provide sample payloads), run both hosted and a temporary reserved pool, and capture latency, cost, and fallback events.
[09:12] Daniel Morales: How do we run the mirror; do you have a proxy or should we replay logs?
[09:16] Marcus Chen: Both approaches work. We can do live mirroring with a small percentage, or you can share an anonymized traffic dump for a replay. Marcus: I'll include a runbook in the pilot plan.
[09:26] Evan Lee: For the pilot, we need to validate KMS integration. Is there a test harness for rotating keys?
[09:32] Marcus Chen: We'll provide a KMS test harness and sample scripts to validate key rotation and audit events.
[09:38] Priya Shah: Ok, what's the rough timeline to get a cost estimate for reserved capacity with our patterns?
[09:42] Lena Park: If you share expected sustained qps and traffic profile by 12/18, we can return a tailored pricing and sizing recommendation by 12/17 — actually 12/17 is tighter; realistically 12/19.
[09:54] Priya Shah: We'll aim to send that by 12/18.
[09:58] Marcus Chen: Quick note about throttling semantics — we support leaky bucket and token bucket algorithms. The Console defaults to token bucket with configurable refill rates.
[10:10] Daniel Morales: Any gotchas when using token cache and KV cache with long contexts? Our prompts can be 8k tokens.
[10:18] Marcus Chen: KV cache is per-session; long contexts increase memory usage. We recommend a quantization-friendly model and region-based routing for larger context runs. We'll recommend quant profiles in the Optimize report.
[10:30] Evan Lee: Do you have guidance on model variants for cost vs latency tradeoffs?
[10:34] Lena Park: Yes, Optimize will recommend model/quantization combos based on your prompt length distribution and latency targets. We'll include that in the pilot deliverable.
[10:44] Sara Ito: Can we get a recording of today's Console demo?
[10:46] Lena Park: Yes we'll share the recording and a short clip of the fairburst simulation.
[10:50] [brief laughter]
[10:52] Marcus Chen: Wrapping up, I'm going to list the key config fields you'll likely change: project quota (monthly tokens), concurrency cap, burst window size, priority tag, routing to dedicated pool, fallback policy, and slices.
[11:06] Priya Shah: For the fallback, can you send the list of compatible models and their perf profiles?
[11:10] Marcus Chen: We'll attach a model compatibility matrix in the pilot docs.
[11:14] Evan Lee: One more compliance question — for Private deployment, do you support air-gapped mode and on-prem image signatures?
[11:21] Lena Park: Yes, our Private option supports air-gapped deployments and signed artifacts. We can discuss that further under NDA.
[11:28] Daniel Morales: Ok, sounds good. Anything else we should know before we close?
[11:33] Lena Park: Just next steps: Lena sends pricing and SOC2 pack, Marcus shares the pilot runbook and benchmark plan, Atlas shares qps and sample payloads. We'll target pilot kickoff week of 12/21.
[11:46] Priya Shah: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[11:48] Sara Ito: Thanks, bye.
[11:50] Marcus Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with docs.
[11:54] [end of recording]

Notes on transcript quality: occasional ASR errors for product names, timestamps approximate.
